text: Why has no demonstrated all-optical switch become the long-sought 'photonic transistor'?
choices: Optical switches are too fast to synchronize with surrounding electronics
Photons cannot be detected at telecom wavelengths
No demonstrated switch simultaneously meets Miller's criteria (cascadability, fan-out gain, input-output isolation, level restoration) at low energy
All-optical logic would violate the Landauer bound
explanation: No demonstrated all-optical switch simultaneously satisfies Miller's checklist (cascadability, fan-out gain, input-output isolation, logic-level restoration, low switching energy), because weak optical nonlinearities force either many photons (high energy) or a high-Q cavity (slow, narrowband, temperature-sensitive). The other options misdiagnose the obstacle, and optical logic does not violate the Landauer bound.
